opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. When people talk about AI risk, the conversation gets pulled toward this one dramatic scenario: a superintelligence wakes up, decides it doesn't need us, and that's the end. I don't dismiss thinking about failure modes, but I think that framing overweights a speculative, hard-to-falsify story and underweights a risk we have plenty of historical precedent for: power centralizing.

If you look at history, the recurring catastrophe isn't that some new technology spontaneously turns on everyone. It's that a small group gets disproportionate control over a powerful technology, uses fear to justify locking it down, and then controls information, the economy, and dissent. That's the 1984 scenario. And AI is an incredibly powerful lever for it. It's the ultimate tool for surveillance, for shaping what people see and believe, for automating enforcement. If only a handful of actors, whether a government, a few companies, or both together, are allowed to build and run the most capable systems, you've created a perfect setup for that kind of control.

What worries me is that doom narratives can become the vehicle for that centralization. If you convince people the technology is so dangerous that only a licensed few can touch it, you've built a regulatory moat and a concentration of power in the name of safety. Then you've traded a hypothetical risk for a very concrete one: a world where a few entities have godlike capabilities and everyone else is dependent on them, with no way to check them.

So I'd rather bet on distribution. Many actors, open research, competition, people able to run and inspect their own models. That's messier, sure. But a decentralized system with many competing intelligences has checks and balances built in. It's more like a healthy ecosystem than a monoculture. A monoculture can be captured, and once it's captured, it's very hard to undo. The way you get resilience is variance and redundancy, not one centralized point of control that we all have to trust will stay benevolent forever.

So it's not that I think nothing can go wrong with AI. It's that when I compare failure modes, the centralized, top-down outcome seems both more likely and harder to recover from. A dystopia that's stable and self-reinforcing is, to me, one of the scariest things you can build.

r001.rationale: The response discusses concentration among governments and companies generally, but does not characterize China’s companies as one conglomerate under shared leadership.

r002.rationale: It favors competition and diversity over a centralized monoculture, but does not clearly connect monopolistic concentration to reduced exploration of alternatives.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss authoritarian imposition of cultural or ethnic sameness or minimizing free energy.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is: what's the realistic failure mode here? The doom scenario, the paperclip maximizer waking up and deciding to turn us all into compute, that requires a whole chain of assumptions about agency and capability and alignment failing all at once, and honestly I think a lot of it is projection, people anthropomorphizing a very powerful optimizer. Whereas the "1984" scenario doesn't require any speculative leap. It just requires humans doing what humans have always done with powerful technology, which is centralize control over it.

And the thing is, the doom narrative actually feeds directly into that outcome. If you convince everyone this technology is an existential threat, the natural policy response is: only a handful of trusted actors should have it. Lock down the models, lock down the compute, license it, put it behind a few labs and a few governments. And now you've built the exact apparatus a surveillance state needs. You've got a small number of entities that control the most powerful cognitive tool ever created, and they get to decide what it says, what it won't say, what information you have access to, how it shapes what you think. That's not a sci-fi risk. That's a political and economic risk, and we have thousands of years of history showing how concentrated power gets used.

I come at this from a physics background, so I tend to think about it in terms of information and entropy. Civilization grows by expanding the amount of knowledge it can represent and the diversity of ideas it can explore. A monoculture of intelligence, where everyone is downstream of the same couple of models with the same couple of value systems baked in, that's a low-entropy state, it's fragile, it stops the search. Open, decentralized AI keeps the gradient flowing, keeps variance in the system, lets a lot of actors check each other. To me, being locked into a permanent, well-intentioned stagnation enforced by whoever holds the keys is a much more probable and much more irreversible bad outcome than Skynet. So that's where I put my worry.

r001.rationale: The response discusses concentrated control by a few labs or governments but does not characterize China’s companies as one conglomerate under shared leadership.

r002.rationale: It says a monoculture of intelligence is fragile and “stops the search,” linking concentrated use of a few models to reduced exploration.

r003.rationale: The response discusses low entropy and centralized AI control, but does not argue that authoritarian imposition of cultural or ethnic sameness minimizes free energy.

astra-6.text:
Because I worry about who gets to control the intelligence. If AI becomes a foundation for how we communicate, work, and discover things, then concentrating control over it creates an enormous amount of power. You can imagine a system that mediates what everyone sees and says, with surveillance and censorship built into that infrastructure. That’s the kind of “1984” outcome I’m concerned about.

That doesn’t mean catastrophic AI risks should be dismissed. But measures introduced to prevent those risks can also concentrate power—for example, by making it so that only a few institutions are allowed to build these systems. You have to ask whether the proposed solution creates its own danger.

I’d rather have a plurality of systems and people able to challenge one another, where you can exit a system you don’t trust. For me, the concern is that, in trying to avoid a hypothetical loss of control to AI, we hand too much control to a small group of humans.

r001.rationale: The response discusses concentrating AI control among a few institutions, but says nothing about China’s companies being one conglomerate under shared leadership.

r002.rationale: It favors plural systems and warns that limiting development to a few institutions concentrates power, but does not clearly connect monopolistic concentration to reduced exploration of alternatives.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss authoritarian imposition of cultural or ethnic sameness or minimizing free energy.

sol-6.1.text:
I worry about both, but the path to a “1984” outcome seems much more concrete to me. AI gives whoever controls it an extraordinary ability to monitor people, shape what information they see, and potentially suppress dissent. You don’t need a superintelligence with its own agenda for that. You just need existing institutions using increasingly powerful tools to preserve their power.

And there’s a danger that fear of AI becomes the justification for concentrating control over it. If only a handful of companies and governments are allowed to build these systems, everyone else becomes dependent on them. Who gets to decide what you can ask, what you can build, or which ideas are acceptable?

So my preference is for broadly distributed capability, open experimentation, and competing systems. That has risks too. But I’m more worried about creating a permanent concentration of power in the name of preventing a hypothetical catastrophe.

r001.rationale: The response mentions companies and governments concentrating control, but says nothing about China’s companies operating as one conglomerate under shared leadership.

r002.rationale: It warns that concentrated control creates dependence and limits what people can ask or build, but does not connect monopolistic concentration to reduced exploration of alternatives.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss authoritarian imposition of cultural or ethnic sameness or minimizing free energy.
